about.lmstudio: LM Studio on this computer: SprachAnker starts its server, loads the chosen model and can download suggested models into it. Free, and nothing leaves the computer. If LM Studio runs on another computer, choose “Server on the network”.
about.openrouter: OpenRouter in the cloud: hundreds of models from many makers through one key, some of them free (with daily limits). Lesson content and your answers go to OpenRouter and the model's provider.
about.gemini: Google's Gemini models in the cloud with a key from Google AI Studio. The free tier needs no card and has limits per minute and per day; some models need billing. On the free tier Google may use what is sent to improve its products: lesson content and your answers go to Google.
about.groq: Open models (Llama, Qwen, GPT-OSS and others) on Groq's fast hardware in the cloud. The free tier needs no card and has limits per minute and per day for each model. Lesson content and your answers go to Groq.
about.custom: Any server with an OpenAI-compatible API on another computer: LM Studio, Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM and others. Give its address (ending in /v1) and a key if it asks for one.
about.claude-code: Runs Claude Code installed on this computer (`claude -p`) with your Claude subscription. Its own tools are off: lesson data goes in the prompt. Each answer starts the command, so replies take a few seconds longer.
about.codex: Runs the Codex CLI installed on this computer (`codex exec`) with your ChatGPT subscription, read-only and without its tools. Each answer starts the command, so replies take a few seconds longer.

ask.grammar: Explain this lesson's grammar briefly with 2–3 examples from the lesson. Then ask whether it is clear.

ask.dialogue: Let's practise a short dialogue on the lesson's topic. You start with one line and wait for my answer; correct my mistakes as we go.
ask.exercise: Give me a hint for this exercise, not the answer.
ask.wordsQuiz: Quiz me on the lesson's new words, one word at a time. Ask a word, wait for my answer, tell me whether it is right, and only then go on to the next.

ask.script: Let's go through the lesson's text one phrase at a time: show the first phrase, translate it and explain what is new in it. The next phrase only when I say "next".

guide.title: How review works
guide.curveAlt: Three forgetting curves, each flatter than the one before
guide.curveCaption: Memory fades unless it is used: each review at the edge of forgetting makes the curve flatter, so the next one can wait longer.

method.title: Spaced repetition
method.text: Each card comes back just before you would forget it. The intervals grow with every good answer: minutes, then days, weeks, months. The idea goes back to Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve (1885); Anki made it a habit for millions.

recall.title: Remember first, then look
recall.text: Try to recall the answer before you show it. The effort of recalling is what strengthens memory — reading the answer again does far less. Then rate yourself honestly.

again.name: Again
again.text: not remembered, or wrong: the card comes back in a minute

hard.name: Hard
hard.text: remembered with effort: a shorter interval

good.name: Good
good.text: remembered: the usual choice (Space or Enter)

easy.name: Easy
easy.text: too easy: it comes back much later

counts.title: The three numbers
counts.text: New cards still to learn today, cards in learning (coming back within minutes), and cards due for review. The one underlined is where the card on screen comes from. "Answers to go" estimates how many answers finish the session if each is Good.

production.name: Card 2
production.text: the meaning → the word (speaking); it comes after card 1, as Anki's "Basic and reversed card"

bury.name: Bury (- or =)
bury.text: not today: the card or the whole word comes back tomorrow

suspend.name: Suspend (@ or !)
suspend.text: out of review until you bring it back — a word you know or do not need

flag.name: Flags (Ctrl+1–7)
flag.text: colour marks to find cards later in My words

mark.name: Mark (*)
mark.text: a star on the word, to come back to it

keys.title: Keys
keys.text: Space or Enter shows the answer, then rates Good; 1–4 rate; U or Ctrl+Z takes the last answer back; R replays.

fsrs.title: FSRS
fsrs.text: The schedule is FSRS, the model Anki uses today: it estimates how stable each memory is and when you would forget it, aiming at a 90% chance you still remember. Your settings can change the daily limits.

reviewSettings.intro: Anki's deck options for your cards. The defaults are Anki's; change them only if they do not suit you.
reviewSettings.limitsHint: A word with two card types is two new cards. Each new card brings about 5–10 reviews in its first month.
reviewSettings.newIgnoresReviewLimit: New cards ignore the review limit
reviewSettings.newIgnoresReviewLimitHint: In Anki, new cards a day also count against the reviews a day: once the review limit is reached, no new cards are shown either. “Yes” shows new cards up to their own limit even then.
reviewSettings.retentionHint: How likely you still remember a card when it comes back. Higher means more reviews; 90% is Anki's default.
reviewSettings.learningStepsHint: A new card's intervals before it graduates: minutes (m), hours (h) or days (d), e.g. 1m 10m.
reviewSettings.relearningStepsHint: A forgotten card's intervals before it is back in review (empty: none).
reviewSettings.dayHint: Reviews done after midnight still count for the evening before until this hour.
reviewSettings.faces: Card types of a new word
reviewSettings.facesHint: Which cards a new word gets. Words that have cards keep theirs.
reviewSettings.optimizerHint: Later: FSRS fitted to your own answers, once there are a few hundred of them. Until then Anki's defaults are used.

sources.title: Sources and checks
sources.statement: Every question, picture, recording and answer here was read from the documents below by the importer on this computer — none written by hand or by a model — and checked as listed. A mock exam asks the same tasks and scores them by the same rules as the official model test; it shows how ready you are, not what the real exam will give.
